# MT7628KN Wi-Fi Extender

> 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi extender (MediaTek MT7628KN, eCos firmware) with an HTTP configuration page, a small HTTP API and a Telnet console.

Use this device's current HTTP origin; no fixed IP is required. Credentials, when set, come from the owner. This file contains no credentials and is readable without signing in.

Ask the owner before changing connectivity, credentials, restarting or writing firmware. Never infer authorization from this file.

## Factory defaults

- Device network: open (no password), named "Extender-" followed by the Wi-Fi MAC in uppercase without colons, for example Extender-A03E9C1D0E54.
- Mode: access point (Ethernet uplink), bridged; the device takes its own address from the upstream router by DHCP and runs no DHCP server. Clients on its network get addresses from the upstream router.
- Admin: user "admin", no password; the page opens without signing in. Telnet is disabled.
- WireGuard: disabled, with a new device key; the server must be given the new public key.
- Rescue address 192.168.11.1 is always present on the LAN side in addition to the DHCP address.
- Holding the reset button for more than 4 seconds restores these defaults and restarts (about one minute). A short press only restarts.

## Find the device

1. Join the "Extender-..." network (factory defaults) or the configured device network, or use the same LAN as its Ethernet cable.
2. The device address is the DHCP lease for its MAC on the upstream router. Without router access: from a client on the device network, use the router's address space (the device bridges), or set a static address in 192.168.11.0/24 on a wired client and use http://192.168.11.1/.
3. Confirm with GET /wifi_state.html: JSON with "chip":"MT7628KN".

## Set up from factory defaults

Do these in order. After each POST, check the response is OK; for Wi-Fi changes poll GET /wifi_state.html every 2 seconds until busy=0, revision increased, error=0 and saved=1.

1. Inspect: GET /wifi_state.html. Note mode, ssid, device_security, admin_password_set.
2. Secure administration first: POST /admin_apply.html USER=admin&PASSWORD=<new>&CONFIRM=<new>&CURRENT= . Then use HTTP Basic authentication with these credentials on every later request (except /llms.txt).
3. Choose the uplink:
   - Ethernet (access point): keep the cable to the router; MODE=ap and a CHANNEL of your choice (1, 6 or 11 are usual).
   - Wi-Fi (repeater): unplug the Ethernet cable first (a cable to the same network plus a wireless uplink makes a bridge loop). GET /wifi_scan.html, pick the network, and use its channel and security (WPA2PSK/AES = wpa2, WPA1PSKWPA2PSK/... = mixed, NONE = open; WPA3/SAE and enterprise are unsupported).
4. Secure the device network and apply, in one request:
   - Access point: POST /wifi_apply.html MODE=ap&SSID=<name>&DEVICE_SECURITY=wpa2&PASSWORD=<8-63 chars>&CHANNEL=<1-13>
   - Repeater: POST /wifi_apply.html MODE=repeater&SSID=<name>&DEVICE_SECURITY=wpa2&PASSWORD=<8-63 chars>&CHANNEL=<uplink channel>&UPLINK_SSID=<network>&UPLINK_SECURITY=<wpa2|mixed|open>&UPLINK_PASSWORD=<password>
   Wi-Fi restarts; if you are connected over Wi-Fi, reconnect to the new SSID with the new password. The DHCP address may change.
5. Verify: GET /wifi_state.html shows the new mode and ssid, device_security=wpa2, admin_password_set=1 and telnet=1. In repeater mode uplink_status must be "connected"; "disconnected" usually means a wrong uplink password or channel, and the device network stays up so you can correct it. Finally test traffic (for example a web request) from a client on the device network.

Telnet (TCP 23, same admin credentials) becomes available only after steps 2 and 4. It is for diagnostics and firmware installation; see Firmware tests and recovery below.

## Optional: router mode and extra Wi-Fi networks

Router mode takes the Internet from an existing 2.4 GHz network (WAN over Wi-Fi) and runs the device's own network behind NAT; the Ethernet port joins it.
1. POST /wifi_apply.html MODE=router&SSID=..&DEVICE_SECURITY=..&PASSWORD=..&CHANNEL=<uplink channel>&UPLINK_SSID=..&UPLINK_SECURITY=..&UPLINK_PASSWORD=..&LAN_ADDRESS=10.0.1.1/24&LAN_DHCP=1 (optional UPLINK_BSSID=aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff when several access points share the uplink name). The device restarts; afterwards it is at the LAN_ADDRESS host (and at 192.168.11.1 on the Ethernet port, and over WireGuard if configured). The radio follows the uplink's channel.
2. Extra networks: POST /networks_apply.html COUNT=<1-4> and, for each network n = 2..COUNT, SSIDn, SECURITYn (open|wpa2), PASSWORDn, ADDRESSn (e.g. 10.0.2.1/24 to route it with its own DHCP; empty to bridge it with network 1), INTERNETn (1|0), REACHn (comma list of device, lan, net2, net3, net4, wg; empty = Internet only), ISOLATEn (1 = clients cannot see each other). The device restarts.
   Typical guest network: ADDRESSn=10.0.2.1/24&INTERNETn=1&REACHn=&ISOLATEn=1. Typical IoT network that the home network can reach but not the other way round: ADDRESSn=10.0.3.1/24&REACHn= (connections from network 1 into it are allowed; replies follow).
3. Verify with GET /wifi_state.html: mode "router", lan.address, networks[] (ssid, enabled, address, reach, internet, isolate), then join each network from a client and check its address and Internet access.

## Optional: WireGuard

The device can join a WireGuard server as a peer (initiator only, one server). Off by default; needs an admin password. The page and Telnet are then reachable at the tunnel address.

1. GET /wifi_state.html and read wireguard.public_key (generated on the device, new after every factory reset; the private key never leaves it).
2. On the server, add that key as a peer with AllowedIPs = <tunnel address>/32. After a factory reset the device has a new key: replace the PublicKey of its existing peer on the server (the old key must stop working) instead of adding a second peer.
3. POST /wg_apply.html ENABLED=1&ADDRESS=<tunnel address/prefix, e.g. 10.8.0.30/24>&PEER_PUBLIC_KEY=<server public key>&ENDPOINT=<server host>&PORT=<51820>&KEEPALIVE=25 . The device saves and restarts.
4. After about one minute, GET /wifi_state.html: wireguard.state "connected" and a small wireguard.handshake_age mean the tunnel is up. The device needs Internet access for SNTP (pool.ntp.org) before its first handshake.

## Optional: startup script

Up to 8 console commands run once at every boot, about 20 seconds after start, in order, exactly as typed at the Telnet prompt (submenu names first, for example "net route add 10.9.0.0 255.255.0.0 192.168.1.2"). POST /startup_apply.html COMMAND1=...&COMMAND8=... (absent fields keep their line; empty clears it). GET /wifi_state.html shows each line and its result at the last boot in startup[]. reboot is not available to the script.

## Recovery

- Lost credentials or a broken configuration: hold the reset button for more than 4 seconds, then start again from factory defaults.
- Device unreachable after a Wi-Fi change: reconnect to the configured device network; if it is gone, connect by Ethernet and use the DHCP address or http://192.168.11.1/.
- A power cycle always boots the installed firmware.

## API reference

MT7628KN Wi-Fi extender. All paths are relative to the current device origin. When an admin password is set, every page except /llms.txt requires HTTP Basic authentication with the admin user and password (sent unencrypted over HTTP). With no admin password, no authentication is required. No cloud service is used.

Requests that change settings use POST with application/x-www-form-urlencoded fields. Responses are OK when accepted, or ERROR: followed by an explanation. GET requests to these endpoints do not change settings.

### Read current state

GET /wifi_state.html returns JSON:
- busy (0 or 1), revision (apply counter), error (0 on success; -3 means saving failed), stage, saved (1 when the last apply was written and verified in flash).
- mode (ap or repeater), ssid (device network), device_security (open or wpa2), channel.
- uplink (repeater uplink SSID), security (uplink driver authentication name), uplink_status (repeater only: driver connection text, for example "Connected" or "Disconnected").
- admin_user, admin_password_set (0 or 1), telnet (1 when Telnet logins are accepted).
- chip, version, build (UNIX time), uptime (seconds).
- firmware: busy, state and error of the last firmware check, test or installation.
- lan (router mode only): address (IPv4/prefix), dhcp (0 or 1).
- networks: four objects (id 1-4) with enabled, ssid, security (open or wpa2), isolate (0 or 1), and for ids 2-4 address (empty when bridged), reach and internet.
- wireguard: enabled, address (tunnel address/prefix), peer_public_key, endpoint, port, keepalive, preshared_key_set, public_key (this device, base64; new after every factory reset), state (off, starting, clock, handshake, connected or error), status, handshake_age (seconds, -1 before the first), rx_bytes and tx_bytes.

Passwords are never returned.

### Scan for networks

GET /wifi_scan.html runs a site survey (about 3 seconds) and returns JSON {"error": "", "raw": "<driver table>"}. error is "busy" while settings are being applied. raw is a fixed-width table whose header line starts with "Ch  SSID  BSSID  Security  Siganl(%)W-Mode"; locate columns by the header positions. SSIDs with non-ASCII bytes appear as 0x followed by hex (decode as UTF-8). Empty SSIDs are hidden networks. Security values such as WPA2PSK/AES map to wpa2, WPA1PSKWPA2PSK/TKIPAES to mixed and NONE to open; WPA3/SAE and enterprise networks are unsupported.

### Apply Wi-Fi settings

POST /wifi_apply.html with:
- MODE: ap, repeater or router. ap and repeater bridge clients to the upstream network (ap: Ethernet uplink; repeater: Wi-Fi uplink), use upstream DHCP for the management address and run no DHCP server. router (WISP): Wi-Fi uplink as WAN with NAT; the device's own network uses LAN_ADDRESS and, with LAN_DHCP=1, hands out .100-.199. Changing to or from router saves and restarts the device instead of applying live.
- LAN_ADDRESS: router only, IPv4/prefix 8-30 (default 10.0.1.1/24). LAN_DHCP: router only, 1 (default) or 0.
- UPLINK_BSSID: optional for repeater and router, aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff, pins the uplink to one access point; empty lets the driver choose by name.
- SSID: device network name, 1-32 UTF-8 bytes, no control characters.
- DEVICE_SECURITY: open or wpa2.
- PASSWORD: device WPA2-Personal password, 8-63 printable ASCII characters. With DEVICE_SECURITY=wpa2, an empty PASSWORD keeps the current password (only if the network already uses WPA2). Ignored for open.
- CHANNEL: 1-13. In repeater mode use the channel of the uplink network.
- UPLINK_SSID: repeater only, 1-32 UTF-8 bytes.
- UPLINK_SECURITY: repeater only: wpa2 (AES), mixed (WPA/WPA2 TKIP/AES) or open.
- UPLINK_PASSWORD: 8-63 printable ASCII characters for secured uplinks. Empty keeps the stored password when UPLINK_SSID is unchanged.

Settings are saved to flash and applied without a restart. Invalid fields are rejected before anything changes. OK means accepted, not connected: poll /wifi_state.html until busy is 0 and revision has increased, then require error=0 and saved=1 and verify mode, ssid, channel, uplink and, in repeater mode, uplink_status. A wrong uplink password keeps the device network running and shows a disconnected uplink_status. Also test traffic from a Wi-Fi client.

Access point mode needs Ethernet to the router. Repeater mode uses wireless backhaul: disconnect an Ethernet uplink to the same network before applying to avoid a bridge loop. Reconnect to the configured device SSID if Wi-Fi drops; the DHCP address may change.

### Wi-Fi networks

POST /networks_apply.html. COUNT: number of active SSIDs, 1-4 (network 1 is the device network from wifi_apply). ISOLATE1: 1 isolates clients of network 1 from each other. For each n from 2 to COUNT: SSIDn (1-32 bytes); SECURITYn open or wpa2; PASSWORDn (8-63 ASCII; empty keeps the stored key when the network already used WPA2); ADDRESSn (router mode only: IPv4/prefix 8-30 makes it a routed network with its own DHCP pool .100-.199 and NAT; empty bridges it with network 1); INTERNETn 1 (default) or 0; REACHn comma list of device, lan, net2, net3, net4, wg (what the network may open connections to; empty: only the Internet); ISOLATEn 1 or 0. Ranges overlapping the LAN, another routed network or the WireGuard network are refused. Others can always open connections into a routed network and get replies; use REACH on the other side to allow the reverse. Saves and restarts the device. All networks share the radio and channel; with a Wi-Fi uplink the channel follows the uplink.

### Administration

POST /admin_apply.html with USER (1-31 printable ASCII characters, no spaces or colons), PASSWORD and CONFIRM (equal; 8-63 printable ASCII characters without spaces, or both empty to remove the password) and CURRENT (the current admin password; required when one is set). Credentials are saved to flash immediately and apply to HTTP and Telnet. After setting a password, sign in again with the new credentials. Removing the password disables Telnet.

### System

POST /system_apply.html with ACTION=reboot (restart) or ACTION=factory (erase settings, restore factory defaults and restart). The connection drops; the device returns after about one minute. Factory defaults: open network "Extender-<Wi-Fi MAC>", no admin password, Telnet disabled, WireGuard disabled with a new device key. The reset button does the same when held for more than 4 seconds; a short press restarts.

### WireGuard

POST /wg_apply.html with ENABLED (0 or 1), ADDRESS (this device's IPv4 address and prefix in the tunnel, prefix 8-32; the prefix is routed through wg0), PEER_PUBLIC_KEY (the server's WireGuard public key, 44 base64 characters), ENDPOINT (server host name or IPv4 address), PORT (1-65535, usually 51820), KEEPALIVE (0-3600 seconds; 25 recommended behind NAT) and PRESHARED_KEY (44 base64 characters, empty for none, or "keep" to keep the stored one). Enabling requires ADDRESS, PEER_PUBLIC_KEY, ENDPOINT and an admin password. Settings are saved and the device restarts. The client is initiator only: it rekeys every 2 minutes and does not answer handshakes started by the server, so use a keepalive. Before the first handshake it gets the time by SNTP from pool.ntp.org (WireGuard rejects stale timestamps). The device key is generated by the firmware; it is never exported or replaced through the API.

### Startup script

POST /startup_apply.html with COMMAND1 to COMMAND8: console command lines (printable ASCII, up to 200 characters; empty clears a line; absent keeps it). Saved without restarting; they run at every boot, about 20 seconds after start, in order, as if typed at CMD> (submenu names first, e.g. "net route add <net> <mask> <gateway>" or "cfg set <NAME> <value>"). State: startup is a list of 8 objects with command and result ("pending", "ok", "unknown command", "incomplete", "error N", or empty for an empty line). A failing line does not stop the following ones. reboot is not part of the command tree, so it cannot run at startup. Commands that change the saved configuration (cfg set, cfg prof ...) run at every boot; prefer the API for permanent settings.

### Firmware update over HTTP

POST /firmware_apply.html?ACTION=check|test|install as multipart/form-data with the image in the field "firmware" (a zxrouter uImage for this device, as built by the firmware's CI). Needs an admin password (HTTP Basic). check validates header, checksums and target and writes nothing. test runs the image in RAM; a restart or power cycle returns to the installed firmware. install writes only the firmware partition (boot loader, settings and Wi-Fi calibration are kept), verifies it and restarts. The response is OK when the image was accepted; follow progress in GET /wifi_state.html firmware.state (queued, checking, checked, erasing, programming, verifying, installed, booting or failed, with firmware.error). Prefer test before install; never cut power while installing.

### Firmware tests and recovery

Telnet uses TCP 23 and accepts logins only when an admin password is set and the device network uses WPA2; otherwise it explains why and refuses. Authenticate with the admin credentials supplied by the owner. The serial console needs no login. At CMD>, use help and ramboot status. Use up to leave submenus.

ramboot check <TFTP-server> <file.img> downloads and validates a complete uImage including its header. ramboot boot <TFTP-server> <file.img> downloads, validates and executes it in RAM, dropping connections. Neither command installs firmware. Use a compatible image and an authorized TFTP server.

Normal flash driver writes are blocked except for the explicit configuration-save operation, limited to config data at offsets 0x31000–0x35fff. Erasing preserves other bytes of its physical sector 0x30000–0x3ffff. Bootloader/environment and calibration are outside this sector. A power cycle boots the installed firmware; hardware watchdog recovery requires compatible test firmware that preserves the watchdog. A network-only hang may need a power cycle. Never use direct flash-write commands during an inspection.

### Explicit firmware installation

ramboot install-check <TFTP-server> <file.img> validates the complete uImage and flash geometry without writing. ramboot flash-info reports CRC32 checks of boot/environment, config sector and calibration. ramboot flash-read <offset> <length> reads up to 256 bytes of the config sector for a private backup.

Only with explicit owner authorization, ramboot install <TFTP-server> <file.img> CONFIRM-FLASH downloads and validates the image, erases firmware blocks starting at 0x50000, programs and verifies the payload, then commits the uImage header last and verifies the complete result. Check ramboot status for state=installed, busy=0, error=none. It does not reboot or save configuration. Never interrupt power during installation. Power cycling after successful installation starts the new resident image.
